title: Revision HQ 2.3: complete outstanding programs
footer: 2.3 Lesson 6: Revision HQ 2.3: complete outstanding programs
starter: A school is about to publish an app written by students. List everything you would check before it goes live.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Lesson 1: Input validation
facts: Validation checks input is sensible before it's processed.
Type, range, presence, format and length checks.
stations.challenge: Explain what is meant by a length check and give an example.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Validation checks input is sensible before it's processed.
Also credit: Type, range, presence, format and length checks.

questions.q: Which check would reject an empty username?
Which check ensures a score is between 0 and 100?

questions.a: Checking input meets rules before it's processed

stations.name: Lesson 2: Defensive design
facts: Anticipating misuse: planning for mistakes and deliberate misuse.
Authentication: checking identity with passwords, 2FA and CAPTCHA.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Anticipating misuse: planning for mistakes and deliberate misuse.
Also credit: Authentication: checking identity with passwords, 2FA and CAPTCHA.

questions.a: Checking a user is who they say they are

questions.q: Which could crash a program even with valid input?

stations.name: Lesson 3: Maintainability
facts: Descriptive names, comments, indentation and white space.
Sub-programs split code into reusable parts.
Makes code easier to debug, update and maintain.
stations.challenge: Describe three ways a programmer can make their code easier to maintain.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Descriptive names, comments, indentation and white space.
Also credit: Sub-programs split code into reusable parts.

questions.q: Which makes code easier to maintain?

questions.a: Code is reused and each part can be tested separately

questions.q: What happens to comments when code runs?

stations.name: Lesson 4: Testing and errors
facts: Iterative testing: during development. Final testing: at the end, before release.
Syntax errors break the language's rules, so the code won't run.
Logic errors run but give the wrong result.
stations.challenge: Explain what is meant by the term iterative testing.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Iterative testing: during development. Final testing: at the end, before release.
Also credit: Syntax errors break the language's rules, so the code won't run.

questions.a: While the program is being developed

questions.q: A program runs but gives the wrong answer. What type of error is this?

questions.a: A missing colon at the end of an if statement

stations.name: Lesson 5: Test data
facts: Boundary: valid data on the edge of the range.
Invalid: right type, out of range. Erroneous: wrong type.
stations.challenge: Suggest test data for an order form accepting quantities 1 to 10.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Normal: typical valid data.
Also credit: Boundary: valid data on the edge of the range.

questions.q: A form accepts 1 to 10. Which is boundary data?
A form accepts 1 to 10. Which is erroneous data?
A form accepts 1 to 10. Which is invalid data?

stations.name: Plan a 12-mark answer
facts: What does it mean to produce a robust program?
Cover validation, authentication, anticipating misuse, maintainability and testing.
For each point, explain why it makes the program more robust.
stations.challenge: Plan the points you would include in a long answer about producing robust programs.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: What does it mean to produce a robust program?
Also credit: Cover validation, authentication, anticipating misuse, maintainability and testing.

questions.q: Which points belong in a 12-mark answer on producing robust programs? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Input validation, with examples of checks; Authentication of users; Planning for misuse and runtime errors; Maintainable code with comments and sub-programs; Testing with normal, boundary, invalid and erroneous data

questions.q: What makes a 12-mark answer stand out?
questions.a: Explaining why each technique makes the program robust, with examples

final.name: Final challenge: key terms

questions.q: Match each key term to its meaning.
questions.a: Input validation → Checking data meets rules before it's processed; Authentication → Verifying a user's identity before they can use a system; Maintainability → Techniques that make code easier to debug, update and maintain; Iterative testing → Testing during development, module by module; Syntax error → Breaking the rules of the language, so the code won't run; Boundary data → Valid data on the edge of the accepted range

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: A program will be used by hundreds of students. Explain the techniques a programmer should use to make it robust.
points: For each point, explain why it makes the program more robust.
What does it mean to produce a robust program?
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 8.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
